body_markdown:
October kept us busy. At NASA Stennis, Terran R’s second stage completed a[10-second hot fire](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7516987162832027648) on A2, the test stand that last supported stage testing during the Apollo program. In Long Beach, stage one integration is nearly complete, with the thrust structure now being mates and the interstage done with structural testing. And at Cape Canaveral, the launch site is steadily taking shape.


**Build**
In Long Beach, the thrust structure reached a major milestone: breakover, which entails rotating it horizontally for the first time. Now fully integrated, the thrust structure houses all 13 Aeon R engines, their fluids lines, and the avionics that control the vehicle in one compact structure.


Completing breakover kicked off mating operations with stage one, bringing the vehicle another step closer to full integration. Getting there took a coordinated effort across tooling, production operations, quality, and manufacturing, along with the teams responsible for every fluids assembly, avionics assembly, and engine.


With breakover complete, the team began mating the thrust structure to stage one, bringing the vehicle another step closer to full integration. Our in-house paint team also began applying Terran R’s livery to stage one.


On the interstage, the team is bonding the thermal protection system (TPS) in parallel of integration and mate to stage one. Meanwhile, welding is underway on the grid fins, the lattice-shaped control surfaces that steer the first stage during re-entry. Terran R’s first stage was designed for reuse from the start, and the grid fins are a key part of that architecture.


Production for future vehicles continues alongside flight one. All flight two engine builds are complete, and circumferential friction stir welds (CFSW) on flight two barrels continue to progress.


**Test** Over at the factory test yard in Long Beach, the flight one interstage completed protoflight testing on our structural test stand, the Tender Loving Crusher (TLC). The campaign applied millions of pounds of compressive load, along with punch loads on the grid fin and loads on the raceway fluids, liquid oxygen (LOX) vent, and nearby composite overwrapped pressure vessels (COPVs). It also applied preloads on each of the stage separation latches. Both the punch loads and latch preloads exceeded expected flight levels. The results confirmed the interstage is ready for the structural demands it will face in launch and wrapped up all structural testing of all primary structures for Terran R’s first flight.


At NASA’s Stennis Space Center in Mississippi, stage two completed a ten-second hot fire on the A2 test stand, the stand’s first stage test since 1970. A2 was built in the 1960s to test the S-II, the Saturn V’s second stage, for the Apollo program. It was later reconfigured to test individual Space Shuttle main engines. Now it’s back in action with Terran R.


On test day, the team loaded propellant and helium and moved into terminal count without a hold. They then fired the Aeon V engine for the full planned 10 seconds. With the stage now in final preparations, the team’s focus shifts to finalizing its configuration to match flight operations ahead of longer-duration testing. That testing includes a mission duty cycle (MDC) hot fire, which will run the stage for the full time it needs to fire in space during a mission.


At the R stand, acceptance testing continues on flight two engines.


**Launch**
At Launch Complex 16 (LC-16) at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station (CCSFS), the team completed steel framing on the launch table. The down conductor towers for the lightning protection system (LPS) also reached full height. Stage two fluids systems are complete in the upper strongback for the transporter erector (TE), and the second TE lift cylinder arrived at LC-16. The TE will carry Terran R from the horizontal integration facility (HIF) to the pad and raise it to vertical on the launch mount. The lift cylinders provide the force that brings the vehicle upright.


At the propellant farms, teams cryo-shocked all liquid oxygen propellant tanks. Cryo-shocking fills the tanks with cryogenic fluid to verify they can withstand the extreme cold before they’re put into service. It’s a key step toward LOX commissioning. And the HIF is now officially wearing our name, with a freshly painted Relativity logo on the building.


A historic stand is firing again, the interstage is cleared for flight loads, and stage one is closing in on full integration. We’ll see you in November!
